page_content: Salesforce Summer ’26: Detailed Developer Release Guide Scope: Apex, Lightning Web Components, Flow, APIs, integration, Agentforce development, Data 360, security, analytics, developer tooling, and related platform changes explicitly described in Salesforce’s Release in a Box – Summer ’26 (v3) . Important limitation: The source PDF is a release-highlights presentation, not the complete Salesforce Release Notes. It identifies major capabilities and architectural direction, but it does not provide exhaustive API-version changes, Apex class or method signatures, LWC module-level changes, governor-limit changes, retirement notices, or availability details for every feature. This guide therefore preserves all relevant context from the PDF without inventing undocumented technical specifics. 1. Executive Developer Summary Salesforce Summer ’26 significantly expands the platform’s agentic-development model. Apex-Related Changes 3.1 Apex Actions as Tools Through Slackbot MCP Client Summer ’26 describes the Slackbot MCP Client as a single interface for an organization’s AI stack. MCP-compatible applications and services can connect to Slackbot, including the Salesforce MCP platform and custom servers that expose: Apex actions Salesforce Flows API-installed tools Salesforce capabilities Tableau capabilities Data Cloud or Data 360 capabilities Why this matters for Apex developers Apex is no longer limited to being invoked from a

metadata.title: Salesforce Summer 26 Release in a Box Summary

page_content: Flows API-installed tools Salesforce capabilities Tableau capabilities Data Cloud or Data 360 capabilities Why this matters for Apex developers Apex is no longer limited to being invoked from a Salesforce UI, trigger, REST endpoint, or Flow. An Apex action can become a governed tool available to an agentic orchestration layer. Slackbot can identify the appropriate tool from a user’s request, route execution, and coordinate it with other tools or agents. Design implications Developers should treat agent-callable Apex actions as enterprise APIs: Give actions a narrow, explicit responsibility. Use clear input and output contracts. Design for bulk safety where the underlying action can process multiple records. Enforce CRUD, field-level security, sharing, and business authorization. Make errors deterministic and actionable. Avoid returning unnecessary data to the agent context. Make side effects clear, especially for writes, approvals, payments, quoting, or external callouts. Ensure actions are observable and auditable. Test ambiguous, incomplete, unauthorized, and adversarial inputs.

metadata.title: Spring 26 Release in a Box Summary

page_content: Mesh, Omni Gateway, and trusted service controls Risks and considerations Operating model complexity: multi-agent orchestration can create value quickly, but only if ownership, boundaries, and escalation paths are defined. Change management: users may struggle if Slack, CRM, portals, and AI workflows all change simultaneously. Governance load: more connected tools and agents increase the need for permissions, logging, testing, and policy enforcement. Data trust dependency: conversational and autonomous experiences will underperform if source data remains fragmented or poorly governed. Recommendation: do not treat Summer 26 as a broad feature activation exercise. Use it to intentionally design a governed agent ecosystem with clear user journeys, trusted data, and defined control points. Bottom line Summer 26 is a more strategic and operationally mature AI release. Its distinguishing strengths are multi-agent orchestration , Slack-centered execution , self-service simplification , and enterprise AI control-plane maturity .
